newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Draft U.N. resolution says Zaire force for 4 months.
newsitem.headline: Draft U.N. resolution says Zaire force for 4 months.

text.p: Security Council members late on Thursday received a draft resolution authorising the humanitarian force for eastern Zaire for no more than four months.

Council members, who were still awaiting a letter from Canada outlining the duties of the force, hope to vote on the resolution on Friday, aimed at averting a human castastrophe by getting food and water to more than a million Rwandan refugees.

Although the force, to be led by Canada, is not organised by the United Nations, all participating countries want the Security Council's seal of approval for implementing the operation. The draft resolution would authorise the mission under Chapter VII of the U.N. Charter which allows the use of force.
The resolution, subject to change, says that the force, expected to number over 10,000, would terminate no later than March 31 after which another operation would take its place.

Diplomats said this so-called "follow-on" force would probably be run by the United Nations and include some of the same troops who expect to go to eastern Zaire shortly. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali is to submit a report no later than Jan. 1, containing his recommendations.
In the meantime, the costs for the mission would be borne by those countries taking part in the operation.
The resolution, obtained by Reuters, urges contributions for a fund set up by Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali to help any African nations who want to participate.

About 1.5 million refugees, mainly Hutus, fled Rwanda in 1994, fearing reprisals after the massacre of up to a million Tutsis and Hutu moderates. The eastern Zairean province of Kivu has remained politically tense since then, with a new war breaking out in September between Tutsi residents of Zaire and local Zaireans backed by Zaire's army.
Diplomats said initial troops expected in the region would come from the United States, Canada, Britain, France, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, South Africa and Senegal.
Other countries expected to join at a later date are Cameroon, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Egypt, Mali, Ireland, Brazil and Portugal. Norway and Finland may send human rights observers.
